facts.statement: Listracanthus shaoyangensis was described as a new species (sp. nov) by Fang et al.
Listracanthus shaoyangensis dates to the Permian Wuchiapingian age.
The type locality of Listracanthus shaoyangensis is the Longtan Formation in China.
Listracanthus shaoyangensis is considered a valid species.
The genus Listracanthus has a fossil range from the Late Carboniferous to the Early Triassic.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Late Carboniferous to Early Triassic

facts.statement: Listracanthus was named by Newberry & Worthen in 1870.
Listracanthus is placed in the order Eugeneodontiformes and the family Edestidae.
Listracanthus species are known mainly from huge feather‑like denticles that can reach up to four inches in length.
facts.quote: Species of Listracanthus are known primarily from their tremendous, feather-like denticles, which range up to four inches in length.

facts.statement: Each denticle has a large central spine with secondary spines radiating from its sides, resembling a feather or comb.
facts.quote: The denticles had a large main spine, from which secondary spines emanate from the sides, like the barbs of a feather or a comb.

facts.statement: The overall appearance of Listracanthus sharks is largely unknown.
facts.quote: The appearance of these sharks are largely unknown.

facts.statement: According to Ray Troll’s account, Listracanthus may have been a huge, fiercely bristled frill‑shark‑like animal with an eel‑like body.
facts.quote: Troll reconstructs Listracanthus as resembling a tremendous, fiercely bristled frill shark.
